extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of literature, and educated readers interested in poetic theory and moral instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for poetry (poesy) focused on its moral, didactic, and aesthetic functions—how different kinds of poetry should work to teach, move, and delight. Intended as high-level craft and critical principles rather than technical meter rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching virtue and promoting virtuous action
rubrics_metrics.description: The final end of all earthly learning is virtuous action; poetry's chief claim is that it most effectively moves men toward virtuous action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet is ‘monarch’ among human sciences because he not only teaches but entices practice: by showing examples and painting actions, poetry moves the mind toward 'πράξις' (action). Examples cited: Æsop, biblical parables, heroic exempla (Æneas, Ulysses) and historical applications where poetic narrative brings moral truths to life. Emphasize making the reader desire to act, not merely know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative imitation: coupling universal precepts with particular examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should give a perfect picture that couples the general notion (precept) with a particular, vivid example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than abstract definitions, the poet supplies images that 'strike, pierce, and possess the sight of the soul.' The painter/painting analogy: seeing a painted beast teaches more readily than verbal description. Use concrete characters and events to embody universal virtues and vices so learners can 'see' the concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and popular instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must be accessible: it is the 'food for the tenderest stomachs' and the 'popular philosopher'—able to reach those whom abstruse philosophy cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive technical abstraction; aim at clarity and forms (tale, song) that instruct broad audiences. Æsop’s fables and simple allegories are models of how to teach common folk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight as a pedagogical strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Delight (pleasure) is a necessary vehicle: the poet must 'give so sweet a prospect' that readers are enticed to enter the path to virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with pleasurable elements (a tale, music, pleasing diction) to lure the reader; hide wholesome instruction in agreeable forms (the 'cluster of grapes' metaphor). The function of delight is instrumental—it produces desire to learn and to practice what is taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of feigned (fictional) examples when illustrating universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Feigned or fictional examples can teach as well as or better than true history because the poet can frame them to illustrate universals and reasonable patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite examples (Zopyrus, Abradatus) showing that a crafted fiction can teach a lesson without being tied to the accidental particulars of history. When the aim is general counsel ('what should be done'), shaping events for clarity and exemplarity is appropriate and often preferable to strict historicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use and defense of pastoral poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral can represent social and political truths via shepherd imagery and lowly speakers; it is not inherently trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pastoral scenes and humble speakers to reveal the misery of oppression and the benefits of good governance; pastoral gives social commentary through simple, relatable figures (e.g., Melibæus, Tityrus). Beware dismissing the form because of its simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of elegy
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegiac poetry moves pity and mournfulness, properly accompanying lamentation and expressing compassion for human weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegiac tone should be used to console, commemorate, and point to human frailty; praised when it accompanies just causes of lament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of iambic verse to chastise vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Iambic verse (satirical iambus) rubs the 'galled mind' and uses shame as an instrument to rebuke villainy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ biting, corrective verse to shame wrongdoing; the function is corrective, rousing moral feeling by exposure and reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire's corrective wit and shame-inducing laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire should 'make a man laugh at folly, and, at length, ashamed to laugh at himself'—using witty ridicule to lead to self-recognition and reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to expose folly lightly but effectively, so the audience recognizes their faults. Satire should combine amusement with moral pressure toward improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as imitation of common errors to deter vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates domestic and common errors in a ridiculous and scornful way so that spectators are discouraged from emulating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray everyday faults, give characters signifying badges of vices (e.g., Demea, Davus), and ensure the representation makes the fault contemptible to the audience rather than attractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s role in exposing vice and moving pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy opens the greatest wounds, shows hidden evils, and, by stirring admiration and commiseration, teaches the uncertainty of fortune and the dangers of tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tragic representation to arouse pity and fear to moral effect: show consequences of vice and the frailty of worldly power; tragedies should lead spectators away from tyrannical or vicious conduct (example: Plutarch's testimony of Alexander Pheræus moved by tragedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric's capacity to praise virtue and raise communal courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyric poetry, by tuned voice and lyre, gives praise (lauds) to virtue and can rouse collective courage and noble feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ lyric to celebrate virtuous acts and to lift spirits (examples: songs of ancestors in Hungary, Pindaric praise); be wary of poetical faults that lie in time/custom rather than the form itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical poetry as the highest kind for inspiring magnanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroical (epic/heroic) poetry is the most accomplished kind: it sets loftiest examples (Achilles, Æneas) that inflame minds toward magnanimity and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present great exemplars in comprehensive situations (war, governance, private virtue) to instruct across many spheres of conduct. The heroical kind is best suited to produce lofty moral aspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere versifying or rhyming: substance over ornamental form
rubrics_metrics.description: Versing and rhyming do not by themselves make poesy; one may be a poet without versing and a versifier without poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the art's substance—imaginative truth and moral efficacy—rather than on mechanical rhyme or metrical trickery. Rhymes and formal prettiness are commendatory only if they serve deeper poetic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with delight, not obscure abstract definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should not begin with obscure definitions that burden memory; instead begin with delightful words, music, and a tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer storytelling and well-proportioned language to technical exposition; tales attract both children and old men, and make moral instruction easier to receive than philosophical abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of music and well-proportioned language
rubrics_metrics.description: Words should be 'set in delightful proportion,' often accompanied or prepared for by musical skill—poetry’s oration refines speech into a high gift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to cadence, rhythm, and musical qualities of language as instruments of persuasion and delight. Where appropriate, combine verse with musical accompaniment to heighten effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing genres is acceptable when each part is rightly done
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poesies couple two or three kinds (tragical and comical, prose and verse); if the parts are good when severed, their conjunction is not harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If combining modes (e.g., tragi-comedy, prose/verse mixtures), ensure each constituent part is well-executed and that the mixture serves the overall instructive and aesthetic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry aims at universals (the reasonable and likely), not merely particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Aristotle, poetry deals with the universal (καθολου) while history deals with the particular (καθ’ ἕκαστον); poetry should present what is fit either in likelihood or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize representing general truths and reasonable patterns of human behavior rather than slavishly reporting particulars. When teaching, frame events as exemplars of broader truths rather than as mere chronicles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid philosophical obscurity: prefer vivid presentation to thorny argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical precepts often teach obscurely and to the learned only; the poet should avoid such thorny manner and make the material evident to common understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on abstract disputations to instruct. Use instances, images, and tales to render the doctrine intelligible and appealing to readers who will not wade through abstruse argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory and fable as potent rhetorical devices for persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables and allegories (e.g., Menenius’s belly allegory, Nathan’s parable to David) are effective to persuade and to make people 'see' their own faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ simple, memorable allegories to achieve moral persuasion—these can produce dramatic changes in public opinion or private conscience because they let people judge themselves in a reflective mirror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral propriety of subject-matter: the poet’s depiction cannot make the thing described evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the poet’s description and end do not contain evil, the thing described is not thereby made evil; poetry’s purposes are to teach goodness and delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects with consideration of their educative ends; depiction aimed at moral instruction is defensible even when it presents wickedness, because the end is reformation and warning rather than celebration of vice.
